claims.claim: Go would be faster [than Node/TypeScript] for in-memory graph work
claims.measured: CPU fib(20) test: go-gin 18,218 req/s and go-nethttp 15,093 req/s, against node-express 7,213 and node-fastify 8,308 (bun-elysia 18,041, deno-hono 14,144)
claims.why: In the closest CPU-bound test, Go handled about 1.8–2.5 times the requests of Node, so the claim points the right way, though Bun on the TypeScript side roughly matched Go.

claims.claim: Node/TypeScript is fine for the serving path (a single keyed read, far below 300 ms)
claims.measured: Single-row Postgres test: node-fastify 9,423 req/s, p50 6.40 ms, p99 14.54 ms; node-express 9,034 req/s, p99 17.28 ms on 1 CPU
claims.why: On one CPU, Node's p99 for a single-row database read stayed under 20 ms, which is far below the 300 ms target.

claims.claim: Does the language matter? Barely. The cost is in data access and the algorithm, not in the language
claims.about: language choice for the recommendation batch job and API
claims.why: Nothing measured a graph batch job, and in the database tests that were measured, languages still differed by more than 2 times (20 queries: node-express 1,062, go-nethttp 2,631, bun-elysia 4,458 req/s), so 'barely' can't be confirmed for this workload.

claims.claim: Loading the adjacency list into typed arrays for 40M edges in both directions takes roughly 300–400 MB, which fits in a worker process
claims.why: The memory figures are for small HTTP servers at peak, not for large in-process data structures, so this estimate can't be checked against them.
